new_statements.quote: There is a phoneme of stress. Intonation often makes it difficult to determine word stress because pitch is raised on the final syllable of a phrase. However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable. [...] The clue may be that when the vowel in the penultimate is lengthened it receives the stress placement, since vowel length appears to occur only in stressed syllables; and when the penultimate is short, stress is on the final syllable. There is also secondary stress and there is length on the vowels of open syllables so stressed. Usually it appears that secondary stress is on the second syllable preceding primary stress, but sometimes it occurs three syllables before, particularly in verbs.
new_statements.citation: Grayden, Bruce. 1979. The Southern Kalinga /l/. In E.C. Johnston, H. Wiens, J.A. Gault, P. Green, B. Grayden & J. Witucki (eds), Papers in Philippine Linguistics No. 9, 91-100. Pacific Linguistics A-50. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A50.91
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.5 STRESS, p. 96 (PDF page 102 of); also sec. 1 p. 92 'Word stress ['] is also a phonemic feature of the dialect.'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (114 pp., Pacific Linguistics A-50, footer on every page: 'Grayden, B. "The Southern Kalinga /l/"... A-50:91-100... DOI:10.15144/PL-A50.91... Online edition licensed 2015 CC BY-SA 4.0... A sealang.net/CRCL initiative'). extracted text of PDF page 102 begins '96 BRUCE GRAYDEN' and PDF page 98 begins '92 BRUCE GRAYDEN', so the locator mapping is right. Viewed the page image myself: section '1.5. STRESS' reads exactly 'There is a phoneme of stress. Intonation often makes it difficult to determine word stress because pitch is raised on the final syllable of a phrase. However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (contrastive) and falls on either the penult or the final syllable; a stressed open penult carries vowel length, an unstressed (short) penult means final stress. Minimal pairs on p. 96: 'ba:lat 'banana' vs ba'lat 'broth'; '?u:tut 'rat' vs ?u'tut 'flatulence'; man'su:gob 'to quarrel' vs manso'gob 'to burn'. This is the standard Philippine penult/ultima contrast tied to penult vowel length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress exists, with length on open syllables so stressed; usually on the second syllable before primary stress, sometimes the third syllable before, particularly in verbs (p. 96).
new_statements.exceptions: Author calls the analysis provisional ('Further study needs to be done on this whole subject'); phrase-final pitch raising obscures word stress; suffixation causes resyllabification and 'stress shift' (sec. 2, p. 98); /a/ reduces to [schwa] in unstressed syllables (sec. 1.3, p. 95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word stress), stated against phrase-level intonation (pitch raised on the final syllable of a phrase); citation-form words with stress and length marked.
new_statements.identity_note: Grayden 1979's data come from Mallango barrio, Tinglayan municipality (note 1, p. 99): 'The term "Southern Kalinga" refers to both the area of the said Municipality, and the dialect generally spoken' there, with minor inter-barrio differences and Butbut (Glottolog butb1235 [kyb]) as the chief divergent dialect. Mallango is an Ethnologue dialect of Southern Kalinga [ksc] alongside Bangad, Sumadel and Tinglayan, so the statement is for the Mallango dialect of sout2908 (Glottolog 5.1 label 'Bangad'), not specifically for the Bangad variety. The same PDF and stress statement were earlier filed under butb1235 as a sister-lect proxy; for sout2908 it is first-hand.
